Why Agents Should Read the Web Like Humans

By Ada Example · September 30, 2026

Most web-reading tools for language models make exactly one request and give up when it fails. That is a poor match for the real web, where the same URL can return a full article, a verification page, or an empty JavaScript shell depending on who is asking.

Start cheap

A plain HTTP request with coherent, realistic headers succeeds on the majority of public pages. It is fast, it is polite, and it costs almost nothing. Only when it fails should an agent reach for something heavier, such as a different client profile or a headless browser.

Know why you failed

When a page cannot be read, the reason matters. A rate limit means wait and retry later. A login wall means ask the user. A Cloudflare challenge might clear in a real browser. A paywall means stop: the content is not public.

  • Retryable: rate limits, transient server errors, some bot checks.
  • Not retryable: logins, paywalls, deleted content.
Escalate only when blocked, and always say why.

Extraction is its own problem. Readability-style algorithms, structured data such as JSON-LD, social meta tags and embedded framework state each succeed on different sites, so the best approach is to run them all and keep the richest result.
